item.title: Tail Instability and Scale Control in Conditional Normalizing Flows for Treasury Yield-Curve Scenarios
item.description: arXiv:2610.14584v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A conditional normalizing flow can produce extreme scenarios even when its point forecasts appear reasonable. We compare two fitted models for daily Treasury yield changes at eleven maturities reconstructed from Federal Reserve curve parameters. Both use an LSTM, an auxiliary location head, and an affine residual flow. On a previously unused 60-date window, the frozen Student-t model generated an absolute standardized coordinate of 34.3 million. A Gaussian-base model with tighter coupling scale control reached 14.72. Each generated 600,000 vectors. The original model's scenario-mean MSE was 33,908.95, while its location-head MSE was 0.3376. The stabilized model's two estimates remained close. Across five development windows, the stabilized maximum was 17.33 among three million vectors. Stability did not imply better prediction: historical simulation had better distributional scores and coverage closer to nominal on the new window. The original flow also had a better log score despite its extreme samples. Frozen-model evaluation is reproducible, but the comparison does not isolate architectural effects or establish a general forecasting advantage.
item.dc:creator: Arin Mohanty

item.title: 4Cast Lab: Open-Source App for Machine Learning & Statistical Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.16800v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: 4Cast Lab is a free, open-source application for machine learning, econometrics and statistical analysis that runs on the user's own computer, with no installation, no programming and no data leaving the machine. It was developed at the E|M|E|F Lab, Department of Economics, Democritus University of Thrace, for researchers, analysts, instructors and students in any field. Its Forecasting mode trains eight learning algorithms (with three kernels for SVM/SVR), implemented from scratch, under leakage-safe validation for time-ordered data; it selects models by cross-validation, compares the selected model with every alternative and with naive benchmarks through formal tests of predictive accuracy, and documents each run in a methods report and a Python script that the user can export. Its Estimation mode covers the core of applied econometrics, from OLS with robust inference to ARIMA, ARDL, VAR/VECM and GARCH. This paper describes the design, the interface and the workflow of version 4.6.2, reports a validation of 1,234 numerical results against statsmodels, linearmodels, arch, scikit-learn and NIST certified values, illustrates the workflow with three examples, and discusses current limitations.
item.dc:creator: Periklis Gogas

item.title: Reinforcement Learning with Hawkes-Structured Networks for Market Making
item.description: arXiv:2610.16524v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Market making under realistic order-flow dynamics is challenging due to the clustered, self-exciting nature of order arrivals, which are naturally modeled by non-Markovian Hawkes processes. We propose a model-free reinforcement learning (RL) framework for market making with general Hawkes order-flow dynamics. We first establish non-asymptotic performance bounds that quantify the loss incurred by approximating the infinite-dimensional Hawkes state using a finite collection of exponentially weighted features. Guided by this analysis, we introduce the Hawkes-Structured Network (HSN), a novel neural architecture that encodes historical order flow through a learnable mixture-of-exponentials filter. HSN is trained end-to-end using model-free RL, jointly optimizing the feature representation and quoting policy directly from reward feedback. Experiments on single- and multi-asset market-making problems with mixture-of-exponentials, power-law, and regime-switching kernels demonstrate that HSN outperforms general-purpose neural architectures, achieving higher trading rewards while implicitly recovering the underlying order-flow intensities.
item.dc:creator: Fernando Acero, Philipp Plank, Yufei Zhang

item.title: GROMM: Generative Risk-neutral Option Market Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.16732v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a statically and dynamically arbitrage-free European option market model with smooth interpolation between option prices, based on the SANOS framework, and prove that its dynamics admit a unique strong solution. In spirit, it is a stochastic model for local volatility when the latter is used as a representation of a European option price surface, not as a pricing model. We illustrate the strength of our approach on S&P Index Option data from January 2022 to August 2025. We show that the model's initial state fits within bid/ask for more than 95% of relevant market option prices. We then train the model dynamics under $\mathbb{P}$ and $\mathbb{Q}$ and show that the model is indeed free of arbitrage while fitting the dynamics of the market well. We also propose a range of BHW-tests to test for absence of arbitrage.
item.dc:creator: Magnus Wiese, Hans Buehler, Blanka Horvath

item.title: A GLE-LSV model with state-dependent leverage and colored noise
item.description: arXiv:2610.18706v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study a local stochastic volatility (LSV) model in which the variance factor follows a generalized Langevin equation (GLE) with colored noise, and past returns act on variance through a memory kernel with state-dependent amplitudes. For kernels given by finite sums of exponentials, we prove existence, uniqueness, and non-explosion under a growth condition linking the volatility map to the potential. In a one-mode family with a polynomial potential, feedback through log returns can cause explosion exactly when the squared volatility factor grows faster than the restoring force. Under structural and nondegeneracy conditions, an exact reduced Markovian state has a smooth density solving a deterministic forward equation. The Dupire conditional expectation therefore requires no stochastic partial differential equation. Under a bounded Sharpe ratio, exponential utility selects the minimal entropy martingale measure, whose premium solves a quadratic backward stochastic differential equation. Under a regularity hypothesis, which we verify in special cases with and without leverage, the premium depends only on the current state, and the squared VIX equals the expected average future local stochastic variance. Finally, a regularized calibration problem with bid--ask constraints admits a minimizer whenever a feasible point has finite objective value.
item.dc:creator: Andrey Itkin

item.title: Real interest rates, exchange rates and growth in three emerging economies: an exploratory analysis of Brazil, India and Nigeria
item.description: arXiv:2410.23002v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper studies the dynamic relationships between real growth, the real lending interest rate and the exchange rate in Brazil, India and Nigeria over 2000-2022. The theoretical framework places these relationships within the literature on the procyclicality of macroeconomic policies, ``fear of floating'' and the global financial cycle, without treating the observed variables as monetary policy instruments directly controlled by central banks. Activity is measured by real GDP in constant local currency (World Bank, NY.GDP.MKTP.KN). Real growth is defined as 100 x $\Delta$log(real GDP) and the change in the exchange rate as 100 x $\Delta$log(exchange rate), with the exchange rate quoted in units of local currency per dollar. The interest rate variable is the World Bank real interest rate (FR.INR.RINR), that is, a lending rate adjusted for inflation as measured by the GDP deflator; it is not a policy rate. Parsimonious bivariate VARs are estimated after examining stationarity, with lag selection by BIC and orthogonalised impulse responses. In the baseline specification, Brazil shows two pointwise exclusions of zero following a real interest rate innovation: a contraction at one year and a rebound at three years. These two features are not, however, robust to the same specification choices: the rebound disappears in a VAR(1), while the contraction is no longer distinguishable from zero when the sample ends in 2019. The estimated responses for India and Nigeria remain imprecise, as do the growth responses to exchange rate innovations. Given the very small sample, the large number of horizons examined, the absence of global financial variables and the non-structural nature of the innovations, the results are interpreted as descriptive and exploratory rather than as causal effects of monetary policy.
item.dc:creator: Hugo Spring-Ragain (HEIP)

item.title: The Fourier estimator of spot volatility: Unbounded coefficients and jumps in the price process
item.description: arXiv:2601.09074v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study a Fourier-based estimator of the spot volatility of a semimartingale, originally introduced by Malliavin and Mancino, and extend its asymptotic theory. First, we remove the uniformly bounded volatility assumption and establish almost sure convergence of the estimated Fourier coefficients under mild integrability conditions. We further derive explicit convergence rates that yield almost sure convergence of the reconstructed spot volatility via Fej\'er inversion. We then extend the analysis to processes with jumps. In this setting, we provide a precise decomposition of the Fourier coefficient estimation error into diffusion-diffusion, diffusion-jump, jump-diffusion, and jump-jump interaction terms, and obtain $L^p$-rates for each component. We show that the estimated coefficients converge almost surely to the sum of the true volatility coefficients and an explicit jump-induced term. Moreover, we prove that an appropriate rescaling of the trigonometric reconstruction yields almost sure pathwise recovery of the quadratic jump process.
item.dc:creator: L. J. Espinosa Gonz\'alez, Erick Trevi\~no Aguilar

item.title: Deep Learning and Elicitability for McKean-Vlasov FBSDEs With Common Noise
item.description: arXiv:2512.14967v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present a novel numerical method for solving McKean-Vlasov forward-backward stochastic differential equations (MV--FBSDEs) with common noise, combining Picard iterations, elicitability and deep learning. The key innovation involves elicitability to derive a path-wise loss function, enabling efficient training of neural networks to approximate both the backward process and the conditional expectations arising from common noise -- without requiring computationally expensive nested Monte Carlo simulations. The mean-field interaction term is parameterized via a recurrent neural network trained to minimize an elicitable score, while the backward process is approximated through a hybrid feedforward and recurrent network representing the decoupling field. We validate the algorithm on a systemic risk inter-bank borrowing and lending model, where analytical solutions exist, demonstrating accurate recovery of the true solution. We further extend the model to quantile--mediated interactions, showcasing the flexibility of the elicitability framework beyond conditional means or moments. Finally, we apply the method to a non-stationary Aiyagari-Bewley-Huggett economic growth model with endogenous interest rates, illustrating its applicability to complex mean-field games without closed-form solutions.
item.dc:creator: Felipe J. P. Antunes, Yuri F. Saporito, Sebastian Jaimungal

item.title: Rough Martingale Optimal Transport: Theory, Implementation, and Regulatory Applications for Non-Modelable Risk Factors
item.description: arXiv:2602.00097v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) poses a significant challenge for exotic derivatives pricing, particularly for non-modelable risk factors (NMRF) where sparse market data leads to infinite audit bounds under classical Martingale Optimal Transport (MOT). We propose a unified Rough Martingale Optimal Transport (RMOT) framework that regularizes the transport plan with a rough volatility prior, yielding finite, explicit, and asymptotically tight extrapolation bounds. We establish an identifiability theorem for rough volatility parameters under sparse data, proving that 50 strikes are sufficient to estimate the Hurst exponent within $\pm 0.05$. For the multi-asset case, we prove that the correlation matrix is locally identifiable from marginal option surfaces provided the Hurst exponents are distinct. Model calibration on SPY and QQQ options (2019--2024) confirms that the optimal martingale measure exhibits stretched exponential tail decay ($\sim\exp(-k^{1-H})$), consistent with rough volatility asymptotics, whereas classical MOT yields trivial bounds. We validate the framework on live SPX/NDX data and scale it to $N = 30$ assets using a block-sparse optimization algorithm. Empirical results show that RMOT provides approximately \$880M in capital relief per \$1B exotic book compared to classical methods, while maintaining conservative coverage confirmed by 100-seed cross-validation. This constitutes a pricing framework designed to align with FRTB principles for NMRFs with explicit error quantification.
item.dc:creator: Sri Sairam Gautam B., Isha

item.title: Post-Rejection Follow-up Sampling: Measuring Outcomes of Rejected Decisions in Algorithmic DEX Trading
item.description: arXiv:2606.08228v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Note (Oct 2026): data were collected by a tracker with a 10-minute sweep, 24-hour cap and one record per token, not the PRFS schedule of v1-v2; headline counts unchanged. Filter-gated algorithmic trading systems on decentralised exchanges reject most candidate tokens they evaluate, yet the observed forward market trajectory of those rejected candidates is rarely measured on the same live venue that produced the rejection. This paper introduces Post-Rejection Follow-up Sampling (PRFS), an observational measurement methodology in which a separate tracking subsystem samples each rejected token's price and liquidity from the same live oracle path used by the rejecting scanner, at a scheduled cadence, from the moment of rejection out to a fixed analytic horizon. The methodology is defined through a formal specification of the observation window and the reason-attribution rule, a reference implementation (prfs v2.0.0) with executable coverage and reason-ledger tests, and a secondary cross-check implementation that re-derives every headline number through a distinct code path. The companion dataset contains 67,000 forward-observation rows across 2,997 rejection events collected on a single Solana automated-market-maker sub-venue during a launch-dynamics window of 8.63 calendar days across 457 unique mints. Under the primary reason-aware three-field event key, 1,455 events (48.55 percent) receive a matched forward observation; under the reason-agnostic two-field diagnostic key, 1,641 events (54.75 percent) match. Mint-level coverage is 100 percent. The 253-row reason-conflict ledger and 8,593 unaligned outcome rows are disclosed, and coverage is shown to be filter-associated (chi-square(6) = 401.29) and source-associated (z = 14.78). No causal or counterfactual claim of a hypothetical acceptance outcome is made; the reported estimand is the observed post-rejection forward return.
item.dc:creator: Arati Uday Kamat

item.title: Inverse Learning of Latent Risk-Neutral Densities from Irregular Option Quotes
item.description: arXiv:2607.27188v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Accurate option prices do not imply accurate recovery of the latent risk-neutral density. We study this distinction with two complementary benchmarks. A controlled benchmark exposes simulator-truth densities for latent evaluation, while a chronological NIFTY benchmark tests only held-out market prices. A two-component lognormal mixture has the lowest aggregate price, $L^1$, Wasserstein, and fixed-tail errors on the synthetic benchmark. Learned operators retain narrower strengths: DeepONet reduces 1% quantile and variance error by 39.0% and 34.6% relative to the mixture, and a quote transformer reduces $L^1$ by 16.4% on the structurally misspecified Merton family. A numerical conditioning analysis explains why these rankings can differ: after enforcing mass and forward constraints, 95 of 126 pricing directions are numerically null, and two densities separated by $L^1 = 0.061$ produce identical prices on the covered strikes. On 524 held-out NIFTY calls, validation-selected test-time adaptation reduces DeepONet RMSE by 28.3%, but per-expiry mixture and SVI fits remain much more accurate. The evidence supports target-dependent inductive bias, not a universal winner.
item.dc:creator: Lennon J. Shikhman, Michael Galarnyk, Aadi Dash, Nicholas A. Welsh
